meta.title: Who really said "Taxes: This is a Question Too Difficult for a Mathematician"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Einstein really did say this. An AP reporter got it in Princeton in March 1944 — though the version you have seen is probably the reworded one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Taxes: This is a Question Too Difficult for a Mathematician'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine. Reported by the Associated Press on 11 March 1944 — but the familiar “it takes a philosopher” wording is a 1963 rewrite.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Asked about his income tax return, Einstein said: “This is a question too difficult for a mathematician. It should be asked of a philosopher.” The Associated Press reported it from Princeton, New Jersey, and the story ran on page 1 of the New York Times on 11 March 1944, the same day in the Los Angeles Times and Christian Science Monitor, and in the Hartford Courant the next day. Quote Investigator ↗ confirms the wording — and shows that the version most people quote is a later paraphrase.
answer.confidenceText: Contemporaneous press report, published while Einstein was alive

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Tax Form Baffles Even Prof. Einstein
Associated Press, in the New York Times, 11 March 1944, page 1 — datelined Princeton, New Jersey
Los Angeles Times, 11 March 1944, page 1; Christian Science Monitor, 11 March 1944, page 8; Hartford Courant, 12 March 1944, page C7
The familiar wording — “This is too difficult for a mathematician. It takes a philosopher” — is not the 1944 text. It first appears in Time on 1 February 1963.

source.excerpt: Asked what his reaction was to the maze of income tax questions, Professor Einstein, whose theory of relativity is supposedly understood by only seven persons in the world, replied: "This is a question too difficult for a mathematician. It should be asked of a philosopher."
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reproduces the Associated Press text and cites it to the New York Times of 11 March 1944, page 1, together with same-day printings in the Los Angeles Times (page 1) and Christian Science Monitor (page 8) and the Hartford Courant of 12 March 1944 (page C7). Its verdict: “There is evidence that Einstein spoke this; however, the precise wording in the original differs.”

Four independent papers carrying the same quotation within two days is strong corroboration of the wording, because it is one wire story rather than four memories. We have not read the 1944 scans ourselves — all four are behind ProQuest — so this record rests on Quote Investigator’s transcription rather than on our own reading of the originals.

The drift is documented too: Time printed “This is too difficult for a mathematician… It takes a philosopher” on 1 February 1963, Reader’s Digest reprinted that version ↗ in April 1964 under the title “The Tax Man Cometh”, and it is the shortened form that circulates today.

We checked the Wikiquote page for Albert Einstein ↗ in full source form; it does not carry this remark in any section, so Quote Investigator is the operative authority here rather than a second, independent one.
source.excerptNote: The Associated Press story as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the New York Times of 11 March 1944. Einstein had been working at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, which matches the story’s dateline.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein reshaped physics with special relativity (1905), general relativity (1915) and his work on the photoelectric effect, for which he received the 1921 Nobel Prize. He left Germany in 1933 and spent the rest of his life at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. His fame made him a magnet for quotations he never uttered — which is exactly why the ones he did say are worth pinning to a date and a page.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: March 1944 was a genuinely bewildering tax season in the United States: payroll withholding had just been introduced by the Current Tax Payment Act of 1943 and millions of people were meeting the modern income-tax form for the first time. A reporter asking the world’s most famous physicist whether he could make sense of it was writing a joke everyone was already living.

The gag in the story is not only the answer but the setup — the AP noted that Einstein’s theory of relativity was “supposedly understood by only seven persons in the world”, and reported that he had called in a tax expert anyway.
detailsBody: The tax expert has a name. Leo Mattersdorf, an accountant and amateur astronomer, prepared Einstein’s returns; a 1985 New York Times obituary records that Einstein was his accounting client for many years, and Einstein read the manuscript of Mattersdorf’s 1952 book Insight into Astronomy.

Mattersdorf is also the source of the other famous Einstein tax line — “The hardest thing in the world to understand is income taxes” — which he reported in a letter to Time in 1963. That one, unlike this one, was never printed while Einstein was alive.
